name: Tadaksahak
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Christiansen-Bolli, Regula. 2010. A Grammar of Tadaksahak, a Northern Songhay Language of Mali. PhD dissertation, Universiteit Leiden. (archive.org item 369-tadaksahak; PDF + djvu scanned text)
catalog_locator: sec. 2.5 Stress, pp. 45-49 (2.5.1 disyllabic, 2.5.2 trisyllabic, 2.5.3 four and more syllables); sec. 3.1.3.2 ex. (12) causative stress shift, p. 56
catalog_quote: Tadaksahak shows clear evidence of lexical stress (cf. also Nicolai 1980). A stressed syllable is realized with a higher pitch and more powerful air stream than an unstressed syllable. Words with four and more syllables may also carry a secondary stress on another syllable. Stress is lexical and unpredictable. Every lexical item has at least one syllable that carries the stress. Pronoun enclitics and grammatical morphemes may or may not have inherent stress. Long vowels do not obligatorily carry the stress. However, when a long vowel is present, the stressed syllable can only be one syllable removed from it. The speakers are aware of word stress and use this feature to create riddles by putting the stress on the wrong syllable to cause the hearer to misunderstand the utterance. ... tone_statements.citation: Souag, Lameen. 2012. The subclassification of Songhay and its historical implications. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 33(2): 181-213. doi:10.1515/jall-2012-0008
tone_statements.quote: Two major subgroupings have been proposed. Nicolaï (1981a:24) divides Songhay into two mutually incomprehensible dialect groups, Northern and Southern; the former he divides into nomadic (Tihishit + Tadaksahak) and sedentary (Tasawaq + Korandjé). The division is justified by appeal to the synchronic criterion of intelligibility rather than the diachronic one of shared innovations. The same work identifies a number of phonological innovations in various subsets of Songhay. Of these, only the replacement of . . . HL tone by penultimate stress supports the claimed division between “sedentary” and “nomadic” NS
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.1 'Previous work', pp. 183-184; the ellipsis '.. HL' is in the original (word-final..HL melody)
tone_statements.summary: Tadaksahak (nomadic Northern Songhay): no lexical tone; where old Songhay had a word-final..HL tone pattern the nomadic varieties have penultimate stress (Nicolai 1981a as reported by Souag) - consistent with the catalog's lexical-stress description (Christiansen-Bolli 2010) and with Tasawaq alone keeping tone.

tone_statements.citation: Souag, Lameen. 2011. Northern Songhay. Online overview and annotated bibliography, sites.google.com/site/lameen/northern-songhay; PDF printout (7 pp., dated 16 Oct 2012) hosted at songhay.org/static/documents/research/.
tone_statements.quote: All surviving Northern Songhay languages have adopted uvular and pharyngealised consonants (except in the latter case for some dialects of Tasawaq), and allow a wider range of consonant clusters than proto-Songhay did. Only Tasawaq retains phonemic tone, although phonemic stress in Tadaksahak reflects proto-Songhay tone patterns (Nicolaï 1981.)
tone_statements.summary: Tadaksahak: no phonemic tone (only Tasawaq keeps it within Northern Songhay); phonemic word stress, its position continuing proto-Songhay tone patterns.

audit.reasoning: The classification (lexical, unpredictable stress with window restrictions in 4-5 syllable words) rests on the modern first-hand reference grammar, which is the top Glottolog source and is held as a text-layer PDF; the deciding quotation and all sub-rules were re-located verbatim at sec. 2.5, pp. 45-49, and ex. (12) p. 56. Glottolog and Persée probed via download). The only unheld items are Nicolaï's 1979-80 print-only articles, which the grammar itself cites as agreeing on lexical stress, and the Köppe edition of the same grammar. Nothing downloaded; our files created but empty.
